title: The four things avoided
hookLine: the Rehat Maryada lists cutting hair, tobacco and intoxicants, ritually slaughtered meat, and adultery; diets differ among Sikhs

cards: Most promises have two halves. A doctor's oath says help, and also do no harm.
A close friendship has things you always do, show up, tell the truth, and a few things you never do, like reading the other's private messages. The yes gives a life its shape; the no protects it.
The Sikh rehat is the same. For five days, the yes: hair kept, a comb, a steel circle, readiness, a sword of mercy. Today, the short list of no's, four of them.

teach.h: KU + REHAT — A BREACH OF THE WAY.
teach.b: Rehat, remember, is the way of living. Put ku in front, meaning wrong or bad, and you get kurehat: a breach of that way. The Sikh Rehat Maryada names four for Sikhs who have taken amrit.

One: cutting or removing the hair, which undoes the kesh. Two: using tobacco. The code also forbids alcohol and other intoxicants, and many Sikhs speak of all of these together: keep the body and mind clear.
Three: eating kutha, meat from an animal killed in a ritual way. Four: adultery, a sexual relationship outside one's marriage. Two honest notes, because this is where people often get confused.
First, on meat, Sikhs differ. Gurdwara langar is, by near-universal custom, vegetarian, so anyone of any background can eat. Many Sikhs are fully vegetarian.
Others eat meat that isn't ritually slaughtered, often called jhatka, killed with a single blow.
Many understand the kutha rule as rejecting meat killed as a religious ritual; it's a rule about Sikh practice, not a judgment on neighbors whose faiths keep their own rites.
Second, the four aren't a list of sins to be scared of. They're guardrails around the promise of amrit.
If someone who has taken amrit breaks one, the tradition doesn't throw them out; it offers a path back, through confession before five Sikhs and taking amrit again.
Keep it clean: the hair, the mind, the table, the marriage.

how: At the amrit ceremony, new initiates are told of the four kurehats from the Sikh Rehat Maryada; gurdwara langar is, by near-universal custom, vegetarian, while Sikhs' own diets vary, from strict vegetarianism to eating jhatka meat.

practice: Think of one small no that protects a bigger yes: no second drink, no cigarette, no scrolling late into the night, no flirting with a line you've promised not to cross.
Choose one, and picture keeping it this evening, calmly, as a guardrail, not a cage. Then rest with the breath, clear and steady.
